source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 2 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section C covers the two threads that run through every engagement, from the first planning meeting to the last workpaper: supervision of the internal auditors doing the work, and communication with the people the work affects. Supervision is how the chief audit executive, or a delegated engagement supervisor, keeps the engagement on its objectives and its evidence sound. Communication is how internal auditors keep the management of the activity under review informed and move urgent or blocked matters to the right person in time. The final communication, its distribution and follow-up are Part 3 topics.
analogy: Think of a film shoot. The director agrees the shooting script before filming starts, decides which crew member films which scene, watches the takes, asks for a reshoot when a scene does not support the story, and coaches the crew afterward. Meanwhile the location manager keeps the property owner informed: a letter before arrival, a walk-through on day one, a quick word when a scene runs late, and a call to the studio head when the owner locks a door the script needs. The studio, not the crew, decides who sees the final cut.

topics.overview: Supervision is the oversight that keeps one engagement on track, from reviewing its objectives at planning to signing off the last workpaper. The chief audit executive is responsible for it and may delegate it to a qualified engagement supervisor. This topic covers the supervisor's four jobs: guiding from the start, coordinating assignments, reviewing workpapers and conclusions, and evaluating the auditors.
can_do: Explain why supervision starts at planning and how its depth changes with the team and the engagement
Assign work program tasks by skill and send a staffing or skills gap to the chief audit executive
Apply the reviewer's test to a workpaper: whether its evidence supports the finding and the conclusion
Describe feedback that develops an auditor without rewarding findings counts or a manager's praise

subtopics.name: Supervision From Planning to Sign-Off
subtopics.definition: Engagement supervision is the guidance, monitoring and review that the chief audit executive, or a delegated engagement supervisor, gives internal auditors from planning to final sign-off.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Work without oversight can drift from its objectives or rest on weak evidence; supervision lets the chief audit executive stand behind work done by others.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 12.3 Oversee and Improve Engagement Performance): the chief audit executive (CAE) or a supervisor guides auditors, verifies work programs are complete and confirms workpapers support results.
The CAE may delegate supervision to a qualified person but keeps ultimate responsibility, even for work done by outside service providers.
Planning: the supervisor should review the objectives; the CAE or delegated supervisor must approve the work program before use and promptly after changes (Standard 13.6).
Fieldwork, should: stay in touch with the team and the activity's management, and monitor that the program is completed.
Extent: closer for a less mature function, a less experienced auditor or a more complex engagement; the Standards set no fixed amount.
Must: the CAE ensures evidence of supervision is documented and kept as the methodology says.
subtopics.example: At a water utility in Lima, supervisor Mateo approves a meter-billing work program only after adding a step on estimated readings. Mateo checks in twice a week with Rosa, a first-year auditor, and weekly with Kenji, who has run two billing audits. Rosa files each dated sign-off in the workpaper index.

review: Compare each work program's approval date with the first test date
Sample closed engagements for dated reviewer sign-off on key workpapers
evidence: Work program carrying a dated approval that precedes fieldwork
Workpaper index showing preparer, reviewer and review dates
Methodology section setting supervision levels by experience and complexity
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set in the methodology how supervision scales with auditor experience and engagement complexity.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive sets supervision methods and stays accountable

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: supervise from planning to final sign-off and keep evidence that it happened. The CAE may delegate the work, never the accountability. How close supervision is follows the auditor, the function and the engagement.

exam_traps.trap: Supervision is one review of the finished file just before the report goes out.
exam_traps.why: Supervision begins at planning, with the objectives and the work program, and guidance continues through fieldwork.

exam_traps.trap: Once the CAE delegates supervision, the engagement supervisor alone answers for the engagement.
exam_traps.why: Delegation hands over the task, not the accountability. The CAE keeps ultimate responsibility, even when an outside provider does the work.

key_terms.definition: The internal auditor who supervises an engagement: the chief audit executive, or a delegate for whom the chief audit executive stays accountable.
How closely an auditor's work is guided and reviewed; it follows the function's maturity, the auditor's experience and the engagement's complexity.

subtopics.name: Coordinating Work Assignments
subtopics.definition: Coordinating work assignments means giving each work program task to an internal auditor with the right skills and time, then keeping the team's pieces joined up.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A task given to the wrong person, or to nobody, leaves a risk untested or badly tested. Named assignments also show who answers for each step.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.6 Work Program): the work program names the internal auditors assigned to each task.
Should (Standard 13.5 Engagement Resources): assign by the program's steps and the time each needs, weighing complexity, budgeted hours, timing, logistics and languages.
May: use the chief audit executive's (CAE's) record of specialist skills; skill assessments also show who is ready to supervise (Standard 12.3).
Must (Standard 13.5): internal auditors discuss inappropriate or insufficient resources with the CAE to obtain them; the considerations make the supervisor responsible for escalating.
Must: an auditor whose objectivity may be impaired discloses it to the CAE or a designated supervisor; reassignment is one option (Standard 2.3).
subtopics.example: Supervisor Ingrid plans a customs-duty audit at a freight forwarder in Rotterdam. Ingrid gives the data extraction to Tomasz, who knows the customs system, and the sample of declarations to Ama. When planning turns up a sub-ledger kept in Polish that nobody on the team reads, Ingrid raises the gap with the chief audit executive instead of dropping the step.

review: Trace each work program task to a named auditor and completion sign-off
Compare assigned auditors' skills with each task's technical demands
evidence: Budget-to-actual hours by task for the engagement
Skills inventory consulted when the engagement was staffed
Record of resource gaps raised with the chief audit executive
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive keep a current skills inventory for supervisors to use when assigning engagement tasks.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive determines how a resource gap is resolved

subtopics.isaca_rule: Every task has a named auditor with the skills for it. A gap in people, skills or tools that threatens the objectives goes to the CAE, who obtains resources or decides the course. It is never absorbed by quietly cutting a step.

exam_traps.trap: Short of staff, the supervisor borrows an employee of the department under review to test that department's controls.
exam_traps.why: That person would assess their own area, an objectivity failure; Standard 2.2 bars even former responsibility. The gap goes to the CAE.

exam_traps.trap: Nobody can do one test, so the supervisor drops it and finishes on time.
exam_traps.why: Standard 13.3 counts resource constraints as a scope limitation. Dropping work silently changes the scope without the CAE's approval.

key_terms.definition: The approved list of steps an engagement will perform to meet its objectives.
A shortfall of money, people, skills or tools that keeps an engagement from meeting its objectives as planned.

subtopics.name: Reviewing Workpapers and Conclusions
subtopics.definition: Workpaper review is the engagement supervisor's examination of the workpapers and draft communications to confirm that the evidence supports each finding, conclusion and recommendation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Workpapers are the main support for what internal audit tells management and the board. A conclusion nobody has tested against its evidence can mislead readers and is hard to defend.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 12.3): the chief audit executive (CAE) or supervisor confirms workpapers adequately support the findings, conclusions and recommendations.
Must (Standard 14.6 Engagement Documentation): auditors and the supervisor review documentation for accuracy, relevance and completeness; the CAE, or a delegate, approves it.
Should: judge whether the evidence is relevant, reliable and sufficient for the objectives, and test drafts against the seven qualities in Standard 11.2.
May: ask for more evidence or clarification. Answered review notes are usually cleared, or a separate record of them and their resolution is kept.
May: supervision includes timely review and sign-off of workpapers (Standard 12.1). A judgment difference follows the CAE's method for resolving it (see 1B4.3).
subtopics.example: In an audit of grant payments at a foundation in Nairobi, auditor Wanjiru concludes that eligibility checks work well. Supervisor Otieno sees the test covered only grants under 5,000 dollars, while the conclusion speaks of all grants, and raises a review note. Wanjiru extends the sample to large grants, documents the results and answers the note.

review: Trace each reported finding to the supporting evidence in the workpapers
Compare review sign-off dates with the issue date of communications
Inspect draft communications for claims wider than the tests
evidence: Workpaper index with reviewer initials and dates
Version history of workpapers amended after review
Completed workpaper review checklists
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive require sign-off on key workpapers before draft results go to management.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive approves the documentation, directly or through a delegate

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: before results go out, the supervisor confirms the workpapers support every finding, conclusion and recommendation. The test is the evidence, not the auditor's confidence, and a conclusion may reach no wider than the work done.

exam_traps.trap: A supervisor who doubts a conclusion rewrites it in the draft report and leaves the workpapers as they are.
exam_traps.why: Workpapers are the primary support for communications. The supervisor asks for evidence or clarification, the workpapers are amended, and the conclusion follows the evidence.

exam_traps.trap: Clearing answered review notes destroys the evidence that supervision took place.
exam_traps.why: Clearing them is usual practice. The evidence of supervision the methodology requires, such as dated sign-offs, is kept.

key_terms.definition: A supervisor's written question or request on a workpaper, cleared once it is answered with evidence or an amendment.
The auditor's own record of the planning, tests and evidence behind an engagement's results.

subtopics.name: Evaluating and Developing the Auditors
subtopics.definition: Evaluating auditors' performance means the chief audit executive or engagement supervisor judging how each internal auditor did the work and giving feedback that builds their competencies.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Feedback is how auditors improve and how the chief audit executive learns who can take on harder work. A badly designed evaluation can also tempt auditors to please the area they audit.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 12.3): the chief audit executive (CAE) gives internal auditors feedback on their performance and on chances to improve.
Must (Standard 10.2 Human Resources Management): the CAE evaluates individual auditors' competencies and helps them develop through training, supervisory feedback or mentoring.
Should: supervision leaves room for constructive comments, written or spoken, in workpaper reviews; meetings during the engagement are chances to train and evaluate.
May: a meeting after the engagement with the CAE; regular evaluations, such as yearly ones, add input. Skill assessment is ongoing, beyond workpaper review.
Should (Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity): the CAE takes care that evaluations do not rest mainly on the reviewed area's input or on findings counts, which may impair objectivity.
subtopics.example: After an inventory audit at a furniture maker in Ho Chi Minh City, supervisor Linh meets auditor Bao. Linh commends Bao's clear interview notes and points to two sampling review notes that took three rounds to clear. They agree Bao will work beside a senior auditor on the next sampling plan, and Linh records the feedback.

review: Inspect evaluation criteria for findings counts or reviewed-area ratings
Compare feedback records with the engagements each auditor worked on
evidence: Signed notes of post-engagement meetings with each auditor
Individual development plans with dated progress entries
Survey results from auditors on their engagement experience
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive base auditor evaluations on the quality and support of the work, not on findings counts.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive evaluates competencies and sets development steps

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: every auditor gets feedback on performance and how to improve. Judge the quality of the evidence, reasoning and communication, not the number of findings or mainly the reviewed manager's opinion. Feedback runs through the engagement.

exam_traps.trap: Rate auditors by how many findings they raise, because more findings show more rigor.
exam_traps.why: Measuring performance by the number of findings is named as an arrangement that may impair objectivity. A well-supported finding counts; a high count does not.

exam_traps.trap: The reviewed manager's satisfaction score should decide the auditor's rating.
exam_traps.why: Stakeholder feedback is useful input, but an evaluation based mainly on it may impair objectivity: auditors could soften results to score well.

key_terms.definition: What an auditor knows and can do, at the level the job needs.
Learning on the job by watching, and working beside, a more experienced internal auditor.

topics.overview: Internal auditors must communicate effectively at every stage of an engagement, not only in the final report. This topic covers choosing the form of each message at planning, fieldwork and reporting, spotting the matters that must move up the line, and deciding who should hear what. The final communication's content, approval and distribution belong to Part 3.
can_do: Choose the form of each engagement message by its stage and weight, and keep a record of what matters
Identify matters that need escalation, such as an unresolved scope limitation, and route each one
Determine who receives each engagement message, keeping confidential information from parties not entitled to it
Tell the internal auditor's escalation steps apart from the chief audit executive's route to the board

subtopics.name: Picking the Right Communication Method
subtopics.definition: A communication method is the form an engagement message takes, formal or informal and written or oral, chosen to fit its purpose, its audience and its weight.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The wrong form can bury an urgent issue in a long email or leave an important agreement with no record. Using several forms keeps management informed and shows communication happened.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication): communicate effectively throughout the engagement.
Should: use a variety of methods, formal and informal, written and oral, such as scheduled meetings, presentations, emails, documents and informal discussions.
Should: the chief audit executive sets quality and content requirements for engagement communications, in line with board and senior management expectations.
How much ongoing communication is needed depends on the engagement's nature and length; its type, assurance or advisory, may change it too.
Should: document the opening discussion in the workpapers; emails, minutes and memos show required communications happened. KaiSip's reading: confirm significant oral messages in writing.

rows.label: Formal and written
cells: Engagement notice, notice of an approved scope change, final communication
Dated and filed; it is the lasting record

rows.label: Formal and oral
cells: Opening meeting, scheduled status meeting, closing communication
Minutes or notes go in the workpapers

rows.label: Informal and written
cells: Email query, short status note, request for documents
Still a record: keep it accurate and objective

rows.label: Informal and oral
cells: Quick question, early alert to a manager
Confirm in writing when the matter is significant

subtopics.example: At a hospital network in Manila, auditor Carmela tells the pharmacy director in a hallway conversation that controlled-drug counts have not been signed for two weeks. That afternoon Carmela confirms the facts by email, copies the engagement supervisor, files the email in the workpapers and adds the item to the weekly status meeting.

review: Sample engagements for written confirmation of significant oral exchanges
Compare opening meeting minutes with the approved objectives and scope
evidence: Emails or memos confirming oral agreements and urgent issues
Minutes of opening and status meetings filed in the workpapers
Feedback surveys from the management of reviewed activities
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive list which engagement messages must be confirmed in writing and filed.

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: communicate effectively all through the engagement. Should: use several methods and match the form to the weight of the message, documenting the opening discussion and other key exchanges in the workpapers.

exam_traps.trap: Informal conversations are not real engagement communication, so they need no record.
exam_traps.why: Informal and oral methods are expected alongside formal ones. The opening discussion should be documented, and records such as emails and minutes show required communications happened.

exam_traps.trap: Telling the manager about a significant problem in passing is enough communication.
exam_traps.why: A significant matter needs a message that is clear, timely and provable later. KaiSip's reading: confirm it in writing and file it.

key_terms.definition: A planned, structured exchange, such as a scheduled meeting, a presentation or a memo, normally kept on record.
An unscheduled exchange, such as a quick conversation or message, used for questions, updates and early alerts.

subtopics.name: What to Communicate at Each Stage
subtopics.definition: Stage-by-stage communication is the planned run of messages between internal auditors and management, from the engagement notice to the discussion of results.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Management needs each stage's messages in time to plan or act. News held back until the end damages trust and delays action.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.1): communicate objectives, scope and timing with management, and changes timely; changes need the chief audit executive's (CAE's) approval (Standard 13.3).
Should: give advance notice as the CAE's policy sets, with the reason, start and likely length, and request the information needed to assess risks.
Should: share the risk assessment results and initial objectives and scope, preferably in a meeting, which also sets expectations for further communication.
Fieldwork, should: give progress updates and raise governance, risk management or control issues that need immediate attention, without waiting for the end.
Reporting, may: a closing communication finalizes results and airs differences; auditors need not change results without a valid reason (see 1B4.3).

rows.label: Planning
cells: Notice with reason, start and length; requests for information; risk assessment results; objectives, scope and timing
Written notice, then an opening meeting documented in the workpapers

rows.label: Fieldwork
cells: Progress, further requests, issues needing immediate attention, approved changes to scope or timing
Informal talks, status meetings and emails

rows.label: Reporting
cells: Results, findings, recommendations or action plans, owners and dates
Closing communication, then the written final communication (Part 3)

subtopics.example: Before a fleet-fuel audit at a logistics firm in Johannesburg, auditor Sipho sends the transport manager a notice giving the reason, start date and four-week length, then opens with a meeting on the risks found in planning. In week two Sipho finds drivers sharing fuel cards and tells the manager that day.

review: Compare each engagement notice date with the start of fieldwork
Trace urgent workpaper issues to the date management was told
evidence: Dated engagement notices and opening meeting minutes
Status reports issued to management during fieldwork
Management feedback on how well they were kept informed
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set notice periods and a rule for raising urgent issues during fieldwork.
audit_focus.decides: The management of the activity under review decides how to act on urgent issues

subtopics.isaca_rule: Communicate early and as you go: notice and an opening discussion at planning, updates and urgent issues in fieldwork, results discussed before the final communication. An urgent issue never waits for the report.

exam_traps.trap: Save a serious control failure found mid-fieldwork for the final report, so all results arrive together.
exam_traps.why: Issues needing immediate attention are raised during the engagement, while management can still act; the final communication then records the finding.

exam_traps.trap: Management agreed the scope at the opening meeting, so a later change needs only a note in the file.
exam_traps.why: The CAE must approve the change (Standard 13.3), and it must be communicated with management timely (Standard 13.1).

key_terms.definition: Advance word to management and staff that an engagement is coming: why, when and for how long.
An early meeting, also called an entrance meeting, to share planning results, objectives, scope and timing with management.
A discussion before the final communication, also called an exit conference, where auditors and management finalize the results.

subtopics.name: Matters That Move Up the Line
subtopics.definition: Escalation is moving a matter that the internal auditor cannot, or should not, settle alone to someone with more authority, by the route the Standards and the methodology set.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A matter left at the wrong level stays stuck. Jumping too high too soon bypasses the chief audit executive and the managers who could fix it.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.3 Engagement Objectives and Scope): discuss a scope limitation with management when found; the chief audit executive (CAE) elevates an unresolved one to the board.
Within the engagement, matters go to the engagement supervisor and the CAE; taking them to the board is the CAE's step.
Must (Standard 1.3): report legal or regulatory violations to those with authority to act, as law and policy set. Sound practice: bypass anyone involved (1D3.3).
Issues needing immediate attention go to management during fieldwork. Which matters reach the board follows criteria the board sets with the CAE (Standard 8.1, essential condition).

rows.label: Scope limitation
cells: Discuss with management; inform the supervisor and CAE
The CAE elevates it to the board

rows.label: Resources inappropriate or insufficient
cells: Discuss with the CAE to obtain them (Standard 13.5)
The CAE weighs the impact with senior management and the board and decides the course

rows.label: Possible impairment to objectivity
cells: Disclose to the CAE or a designated supervisor (Standard 2.3)
If it affects the work, the CAE discusses it with the parties concerned and decides

rows.label: Risk accepted above appetite or tolerance
cells: Bring the facts to the supervisor or CAE
The CAE discusses it with senior management, then the board if unresolved (Standard 11.5)

rows.label: Disagreement on the results
cells: Discuss, seek mutual understanding, record both positions (Standard 13.1)
The CAE should work with senior management (Standard 14.4); the board gets the facts if the function's work is affected (Standard 8.1)

subtopics.example: In a warehouse safety audit at a mining supplier in Perth, auditor Liam finds a fire exit chained shut and tells the site manager at once, confirming by email. The same manager refuses to release forklift incident logs. Liam explains why they are needed, is refused again, records the refusal and reports it to the engagement supervisor and the chief audit executive.

review: Trace each recorded scope limitation to its discussion and outcome
Compare dates matters were found with dates they were escalated
evidence: Escalation log listing matter, date raised, recipient and outcome
Board minutes recording scope limitations the chief audit executive elevated
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive write escalation triggers and routes into the methodology, agreed with the board.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides whether to intervene in matters the chief audit executive elevates

subtopics.isaca_rule: Route by the matter: a scope limitation to management, then the CAE elevates it; resource gaps and impairments to the CAE; violations to those with authority to act. Reaching the board is the CAE's step, and urgent issues never wait.

exam_traps.trap: An auditor refused access by a manager writes at once to the audit committee chair.
exam_traps.why: A scope limitation is first discussed with management to resolve it. If that fails, the CAE elevates it to the board.

exam_traps.trap: A scope limitation recorded in the workpapers has been dealt with.
exam_traps.why: Recording it is only the start: it must be discussed with management, and an unresolved one goes from the CAE to the board.

key_terms.definition: Passing a matter to a higher authority because the current level cannot, or should not, settle it.
The rules the board sets with the chief audit executive for which issues reach the board, such as significant risks above its tolerance.

subtopics.name: Choosing Who Hears What
subtopics.definition: Choosing recipients means deciding, for each engagement message, who needs it to plan, act or oversee, and keeping it from anyone not entitled to see it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A message sent to the wrong person does nothing or does harm: a finding nobody can act on, a leaked draft, a warning to the person involved.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.1): the management of the activity under review hears the objectives, scope and timing, and any later changes.
Should (Standard 14.4 Recommendations and Action Plans): discuss findings and possible recommendations promptly with the managers authorized to make changes.
Advisory work: nature and scope may be agreed with the requesting party, and the work program should be built with them (Domain V introduction; Standard 13.6).
Must (Standard 5.2 Protection of Information): confidential information goes only to authorized people, unless a legal or professional duty requires disclosure.
Must (Standard 11.3): the CAE decides who receives the final communication and, as required, seeks legal or senior management advice before an outside release.
subtopics.example: Auditor Hamid is reviewing vendor onboarding at a telecom company in Casablanca. The procurement director, who can change the process, asks Hamid to email the draft findings to a vendor's lawyer. Hamid discusses the findings with the director but sends nothing outside, explaining that any outside release is the chief audit executive's decision.

review: Compare distribution lists with the recipients agreed at the opening meeting
Trace each release of engagement records outside to its approval
evidence: Distribution records for engagement communications, with dates
Approval records for outside releases, with legal counsel's advice
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive define in the methodology which management level receives each kind of engagement communication.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides who receives the final communication

subtopics.isaca_rule: Send each message to the people who need it to act or oversee, at the level with authority to change the process. Confidential information goes only to authorized parties; the final communication's distribution is the CAE's decision.

exam_traps.trap: Discuss findings first with the staff member whose work was tested, since they know the process best.
exam_traps.why: Staff can confirm facts, but findings and possible recommendations should go to the managers with authority to change the activity.

exam_traps.trap: The internal auditor may send results to the regulator who asked, to save time.
exam_traps.why: An outside release is the CAE's decision, after legal or senior management advice unless law says otherwise.

key_terms.term: Management of the activity under review
key_terms.definition: The managers who run the area being examined and who own its processes, controls and actions.
The stakeholder who asks for an advisory service and agrees its nature and scope.
Anyone without a right, under policy or law, to receive the information.

key_terminologies.Chief audit executive (CAE): The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
key_terminologies.Engagement supervisor: The internal auditor who supervises an engagement: the chief audit executive, or a delegate for whom the chief audit executive stays accountable.
key_terminologies.Extent of supervision: How closely an auditor's work is guided and reviewed; it follows the function's maturity, the auditor's experience and the engagement's complexity.
key_terminologies.Work program: The approved list of steps an engagement will perform to meet its objectives.
key_terminologies.Resource limitation: A shortfall of money, people, skills or tools that keeps an engagement from meeting its objectives as planned.
key_terminologies.Review note: A supervisor's written question or request on a workpaper, cleared once it is answered with evidence or an amendment.
key_terminologies.Workpapers: The auditor's own record of the planning, tests and evidence behind an engagement's results.
key_terminologies.Competency: What an auditor knows and can do, at the level the job needs.
key_terminologies.Mentoring: Learning on the job by watching, and working beside, a more experienced internal auditor.
key_terminologies.Methodologies: The chief audit executive's documented way of working, which internal auditors follow.
key_terminologies.Formal communication: A planned, structured exchange, such as a scheduled meeting, a presentation or a memo, normally kept on record.
key_terminologies.Informal communication: An unscheduled exchange, such as a quick conversation or message, used for questions, updates and early alerts.
key_terminologies.Engagement notice: Advance word to management and staff that an engagement is coming: why, when and for how long.
key_terminologies.Opening meeting: An early meeting, also called an entrance meeting, to share planning results, objectives, scope and timing with management.
key_terminologies.Closing communication: A discussion before the final communication, also called an exit conference, where auditors and management finalize the results.
key_terminologies.Final communication: The communication issued at the end of an engagement with its results, often a written report.
key_terminologies.Escalation: Passing a matter to a higher authority because the current level cannot, or should not, settle it.
key_terminologies.Escalation criteria: The rules the board sets with the chief audit executive for which issues reach the board, such as significant risks above its tolerance.
key_terminologies.Scope limitation: A condition in an assurance engagement, such as restricted access, that prevents the planned work.
key_terminologies.Management of the activity under review: The managers who run the area being examined and who own its processes, controls and actions.
key_terminologies.Requesting party: The stakeholder who asks for an advisory service and agrees its nature and scope.
key_terminologies.Unauthorized party: Anyone without a right, under policy or law, to receive the information.
